header:
Date: 2025-10-21
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Emily Zhang (AtlasRetail Head of ML), Mark Rivera (AtlasRetail Platform), Sana Khan (AtlasRetail CTO)
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood Optimize recommendations focused on batching and prefix/KV cache. Discussed expected latency/cost tradeoffs, cache hit-rate assumptions, recommended batching window and max batch sizes, and a simple cost-savings model. Agreed next steps to exchange traces and run benchmarks.
topics: Prefix / KV cache behavior and hit-rate assumptions
Cost model and expected token savings
Tradeoffs: latency vs cost, cold starts, TTL and eviction policies
transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, we'll do a 40-ish minute walkthrough of Optimize — specifically batching and the prefix / KV cache cost model. My name's Avery, I'm the AE, Diego is our SE.
[00:12] Diego Morales: Hey hi, thanks. We'll start with a short overview then dig into your request patterns and show the spreadsheet.
[00:20] Emily Zhang: Thanks, hey — quick note, we have to keep this high level until legal signs the NDA but we're excited to see the cost work.
[00:28] Avery Chen: Totally understood. Quick ask — who on your side owns the request traces / logs and could share a sample distribution of sequence lengths?
[00:36] Mark Rivera: That's me, Mark. I can pull recent traces. Our typical request seq length is 40 tokens mean, but there are tails up to 1,200 with summarization jobs.
[00:46] Diego Morales: That's helpful. So we'll show two recommendations: a conservative batching policy for latency-sensitive routes, and a throughput-focused policy with aggressive batching for background jobs.
[00:58] Avery Chen: First, prefix vs KV cache — quick primer: prefix caching is for repeated initial tokens (like prompts, instructions) so you avoid redoing the forward pass for that prefix; KV cache stores per-request key/value states to accelerate autoregressive sampling when continuation requests happen. Both reduce compute but have different hit profiles.
[01:18] Emily Zhang: Is that the same as what some folks call "prompt caching"?
[01:22] Diego Morales: Yeah, prompt cache roughly. Sometimes the nouns get swapped in transcripts, so apologies if we say KV cache and mean prefix, but the distinction is important operationally.
[01:32] [01:33] Sana Khan: We care about PII — will cached prefixes or KV caches store customer text? We need KMS + TTL and clear audit logs.
[01:39] Avery Chen: Good question. You can configure the cache to store opaque embeddings or encrypted blobs. In Redwood Private / Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS; audit logs are available and we redact full text by default at rest unless you opt in.
[01:52] Diego Morales: Back to batching: the two axes are max batch size and batch latency window (the time we wait to fill a batch). For latency-sensitive API routes we recommend a small timeout, e.g., 10-30ms and max batch size 16-32 depending on model and GPU. For background jobs, we increase the timeout to 100-200ms and bump batch size to 64-256.
[02:18] Mark Rivera: How do you pick the timeout? if we set it too high client will see bad p95s.
[02:24] Diego Morales: Right — we optimize for p50 vs p95. The rule of thumb: choose a timeout such that average request arrival will fill a good portion of the batch within the timeout. If your QPS per route is low, prefer smaller timeout + smaller max batch, and rely on KV cache for cost savings.
[02:40] Emily Zhang: And how does KV cache interplay with batching? If you have high cache hit-rate does batching still help?
[02:47] Diego Morales: Great question. If a request hits the prefix cache we skip full prefix computation, so the per-token cost goes down; batching still helps for the remaining autoregressive tokens because the attention and GEMM ops are still batched across examples. But the effective batch size (compute weight) is lower when prefix reduces work, so you may be able to increase max batch size for cached requests.
[03:08] Avery Chen: We ran a simple model: baseline no cache, batch window 20ms, batch size 32 on an A100-like profile — then enabled prefix cache with a conservative 60% hit-rate, and we saw token compute drop ~45% and cost per request down ~38% in the spreadsheet we shared.
[03:26] Mark Rivera: Where did the 60% number come from? Our sessions have a lot of unique user inputs, maybe lower hit rates.
[03:33] Diego Morales: It's an assumption for canonical chat use, but the spreadsheet includes sensitivity scenarios: 20%, 40%, 60%, 80% hit rates. We can plug in your traces to get a realistic projection.
[03:47] [03:48] Emily Zhang: Can you show the cost model now?
[03:50] Diego Morales: Yup — pulling the shared sheet. (pauses) Ok so column A is request type, column B mean seq length, C baseline tokens, D compute cost per token, E batch policy, F assumed cache hit-rate, G effective tokens executed, H cost per request, I percent savings.
[04:12] Diego Morales: Example: conversational route, mean 40 tokens, 60% prefix hit, baseline 40 token compute -> effective 16, batching gives 20% additional efficiency so cost per request goes from $0.012 to $0.007 => 42% savings.
[04:29] Sana Khan: Those absolute numbers look good, but we need to validate at scale — our peak concurrency hits memory limits on cheaper GPUs.
[04:36] Avery Chen: For Dedicated we let you pin instance types; the Optimize recommendations include quantization and kernel selection suggestions per model. If memory is constrained, you can use int8 or 4-bit quantization which we estimate to reduce memory footprint ~2-3x.
[04:51] Mark Rivera: Is quantization supported across all models? We rely on some Llama variants and also a couple proprietary models.
[04:57] Diego Morales: Most of the open Llama-family models we onboarded support 8-bit and 4-bit quantized kernels in our runtime; proprietary models can be tested — we do a quick compatibility pass during model onboarding.
[05:07] Emily Zhang: Walk me through TTL and eviction behavior for prefix cache. We don't want stale instructions staying forever.
[05:13] Diego Morales: TTL is configurable at route-level. Recommended defaults: short-lived instruction caches (e.g., 1h) for ephemeral prompts; longer TTL for known system prompts (24h). Eviction uses LRU with size caps; we also expose metrics for cache hit-rate, eviction rate, and memory usage in the Console.
[05:31] Avery Chen: A caveat: prefix cache works best when a lot of traffic repeats the same instruction/prompt. If your users' prompts vary a lot, KV caching across continuation tokens (for follow-up calls) often yields bigger wins.
[05:44] Mark Rivera: About cold-starts: do you pre-warm the cache or the model? In Dedicated we can have warm pools?
[05:50] Diego Morales: Yes, Dedicated offers warm pools and we can keep a fraction of replicas warmed with prefetched popular prefixes. For hosted we rely on rapid model loading + ephemeral warmups; the Optimize suggestions flag hot prefixes so you can proactively pin them.
[06:02] Emily Zhang: On metrics — what do you surface for debugging cost regressions?
[06:06] Avery Chen: In the Console: per-route token counts, cache hit-rate, batch sizes distribution, p50/p95 latencies, and per-token cost breakdown. We also emit traces you can ingest into your APM.
[06:18] Mark Rivera: One of our concerns is embedding cache vs KV cache confusion — does Redwood support embedding reuse?
[06:24] Diego Morales: Yes embedding caching is separate; Optimize can suggest caching embeddings for repeated similarity lookups, with TTLs and size caps, and that's in the same cost model sheet but a different line item.
[06:34] [06:36] Sana Khan: Security again: who can access audit logs, can we map to SSO groups?
[06:40] Avery Chen: RBAC is SAML-enabled, and audit logs are exportable to your SIEM. We can provide SOC2 docs as part of the SSO + Private deployment conversations.
[06:51] Diego Morales: Back to numbers — here's a simple sensitivity table: with a 20% hit-rate savings are modest (10-15%), at 40% you see 25-30% savings, at 60% 35-45% savings. The crossover is often around 30-35% depending on batching efficiency and sequence lengths.
[07:12] Mark Rivera: Does the cost model account for memory overhead of keeping large KV caches? If we keep per-customer session caches for long TTLs we might need more RAM.
[07:20] Diego Morales: We have a line item for cache RAM cost in the sheet — you can assign $/GB-month for your infra. The model then calculates net savings after amortized memory cost. In many cases net is still strongly positive for active customers but less so for very low QPS routes.
[07:35] Emily Zhang: Let's talk POC: we can share traces and a small dev cluster. We want to see baseline, cached, and tuned batching numbers. What's a realistic scope for a 2-4 hour benchmark?
[07:44] Avery Chen: Diego — walkthrough the suggested benchmark.
[07:46] Diego Morales: Sure: 1) Provide 1-2 days of request traces (anonymized). 2) We'll run three runs: baseline (no cache, conservative batching), prefixed cache enabled, and tuned batching + cache enabled. Each run ~30-60 minutes to get stable metrics. We'll capture p50/p95, throughput, tokens/sec, and cost per 1k requests. We'll deliver a CSV and updated cost model.
[08:09] Mark Rivera: That sounds good. For traces we will redact user IDs but keep session IDs to see continuation patterns.
[08:15] Avery Chen: Perfect. Next steps recap: Avery will share the spreadsheet and a short guide; Diego will run the bench once Mark shares traces; Mark to send traces by Friday.
[08:26] Emily Zhang: Quick question — any gotchas with function calling and caching? Does tool calling break cache assumptions?
[08:33] Diego Morales: Function/tool calls usually change downstream tokens; prefix cache can still save upstream instruction work if tool calls are appended after cached prefix. But you should avoid caching outputs that contain tool-returned PII. We have route-level flags to disable caching for those patterns.
[08:49] Sana Khan: If we go private, how long to set up a Dedicated environment for a POC? We prefer Dedicated for predictable perf.
[08:55] Avery Chen: For Dedicated POC we can usually provision a small pool in 1-2 weeks depending on legal/compliance reviews. Private on-prem takes longer — typically 4-8 weeks.
[09:06] Mark Rivera: Are there any limitations on concurrency per GPU we should be aware of?
[09:10] Diego Morales: Concurrency is bounded by memory and KV cache size; Optimize will recommend concurrency caps per model/hardware combo. For example on an 80GB card with a Llama-13B quantized to 4-bit we typically recommend concurrency 8-16 depending on seq len.
[09:25] Emily Zhang: Okay thanks. From my side, we'll prioritize sending traces and an initial list of priority routes.
[09:31] Avery Chen: Awesome. We'll follow up with the spreadsheet and kickoff email. Thanks everyone.
[09:35] Diego Morales: Thanks all, bye.
[09:37] [call ends]

Notes: transcription has occasional mislabels; some technical nouns may be abbreviated. The team agreed on a concrete POC scope and timeline.
